before.title: AMC 20 rear axle — weak two-piece axle shafts (spun hub / sheared key)
before.description: The factory AMC Model 20 rear axle uses a two-piece axle shaft: a splined shaft with a separate pressed-on hub retained by a Woodruff key and a single large nut. The hub is held by the spline taper and the torque of that nut — the small key only indexes the splines, it doesn't carry load. If the nut backs off or was never torqued to spec, the hub spins on the shaft, chews out the keyway, and the wheel/hub can walk off the axle entirely. It is one of the best-known CJ failure modes and a real safety issue, especially with bigger tires.
before.solution: The accepted bulletproofing fix is a one-piece axle conversion kit (Yukon, Alloy USA, Omix — sold per model year and for Quadra-Trac vs standard housings). It replaces both two-piece shafts with forged 29-spline one-piece axles plus new bearings, seals, retainers and studs, eliminating the spinning-hub failure entirely. Restorers staying stock instead replace any shaft with a damaged keyway, fit fresh hubs, and torque the hub nut to the factory ~250 ft-lb spec with a new cotter pin (never backing the nut off to line up the pin). For heavily-built rigs the whole AMC 20 is sometimes swapped for a Dana 44.
symptoms: Clicking or clunking from the rear hub under load
Wheel wobble or the hub working loose
Chewed-up keyway or stripped splines when the hub is pulled
Wheel/hub separating from the axle in severe cases
Rear-axle play that returns shortly after retorquing the nut

before.title: Body tub, floor pans, rockers and firewall rust
before.description: CJ-7 tubs are unprotected stamped steel and the body sits in standing water any time the soft top leaks or the drain holes plug. Corrosion concentrates in the front and rear floor pans, the seat risers, the rocker/sill panels, the wheel-well lips, the cowl/firewall, and the body-mount cups where the tub bolts to the frame. Once the body mounts and floor rot, the tub can no longer locate properly on the frame, doors/tailgate stop lining up, and the whole structure flexes.
before.solution: The community fix is die-stamped factory-gauge replacement panels rather than hand-formed patches: EDP-coated front and rear floor pans, rockers, wheelhouses and cowl repair sections (Key Parts/Quadratec, Classic 2 Current Fabrication) welded in after the rot is cut back to clean steel. Restorers replace the body-mount cups and use new polyurethane body-mount bushings, then seam-seal and undercoat the underside and brush cavity wax into the rockers and tub seams. When the tub is too far gone, a full reproduction steel tub (firewall-to-tailgate) from Willys-Overland/Repli-Tub is the reliable path. Keeping the drain plugs clear and the top sealed prevents a repeat.
symptoms: Soft, crunchy or holed floor under the carpet/mats
Rusted-through rockers and rear wheel-well lips
Doors and tailgate no longer aligning or latching
Body shifting or squeaking on the frame from rotted mounts
Bubbling paint along the cowl and seat risers

before.title: Carter BBD carburetor & emissions vacuum maze (rough idle, stalling)
before.description: Smog-era 258 CJ-7s run the two-barrel Carter BBD feeding a sprawling emissions vacuum system (CTO switches, ported vacuum, stepper-motor/feedback control on later cars). The BBD is dirt-sensitive and drifts out of tune; combined with cracked decades-old vacuum hoses and missing/disconnected emissions components it produces chronic rough idle, idle hunting/runaway, stalling, backfiring and poor mileage. On a restoration the half-rotted vacuum diagram is usually undecipherable, and a worn BBD with a wrong float level (often set to 3/8" instead of the correct ~1/4") never idles right.
before.solution: Restorers either properly rebuild the BBD (new kit, correct float level, clean every passage) and renew the entire vacuum harness off a correct year diagram, or — the popular bulletproofing route — convert to a non-feedback carb and delete the computer/emissions tangle. Common swaps are a Motorcraft/Carter 2100-style two-barrel or a Weber 38 with a simple adapter, paired with the HEI ignition so the ECU, stepper motor and most vacuum lines can be removed for a clean, tunable, reliable setup. Many also add a quality fuel filter and rebuild the mechanical pump as part of the job.
symptoms: Rough or hunting idle, idle runaway to high rpm
Stalling at idle or when coming off throttle
Backfiring and hesitation
Poor fuel economy and black smoke (over-rich)
Vacuum leaks from cracked/missing emissions hoses

before.title: Frame rot at the rear spring hangers, shackle mounts and skid-plate area
before.description: The CJ-7's boxed steel frame is thin-wall and ungalvanized, and the boxed rear sections trap mud and water with no good way to drain. Rot concentrates at the rear leaf-spring hangers/shackle mounts, the rear crossmember, the body-mount tabs, and around the fuel-tank skid plate behind the rear wheels. Because the rails are boxed, the inside rusts from the inside out, so a frame that looks paintable on the surface can be paper-thin internally — the classic failure is a spring hanger or shackle mount tearing away, which is a structural/safety defect, not a cosmetic one.
before.solution: Restorers do a frame-off, media-blast or wire-wheel the bare frame, then probe/sound the boxed sections for hidden rot. Rotted spring-hanger, shackle and crossmember areas are cut out and replaced with weld-in repair sections (Rust Buster, Quadratec and others sell CJ-specific boxed hanger and crossmember plates) rather than just plated over. The proven longevity step is to internally treat the boxed rails after repair — flush, dry, and flood the inside with cavity/penetrating wax (e.g. Fluid Film, Woolwax or POR-15 cavity wax) through drilled access holes, then seal the outside with epoxy primer and chassis coating. Badly-gone frames get a new aftermarket reproduction frame.
symptoms: Flaky or bubbling paint over the rear frame rails
Soft or perforated metal you can push a screwdriver through near the rear spring hangers
Clunking or shifting feel from a loose/torn shackle or hanger mount
Crooked stance or body shifting on the frame
Visible rot around the fuel-tank skid plate

before.title: Vague steering / death wobble from worn linkage and geometry
before.description: The CJ-7's leaf-sprung solid front axle with a long drag link and exposed tie-rod ends is prone to wander and to 'death wobble' — a violent self-sustaining shimmy of the front end triggered by a bump. Causes are worn tie-rod/drag-link ends, tired spring bushings and shackles, loose wheel bearings, and incorrect caster (often after a lift). The factory linkage is thin-wall and the steering-box mount can flex, so as the parts age the Jeep gets darty on-road and unstable at speed.
before.solution: The community cure is a systematic refresh: replace all four tie-rod/drag-link ends, the spring bushings and shackles, and set wheel-bearing preload, then verify caster (a degreed shim or correcting the drag-link/tie-rod geometry on lifted rigs — the 'rod flip'). The durable upgrade is a heavy-duty tie rod and drag link kit (e.g. 1-1/8" x .250-wall DOM, several times stronger than stock) plus a steering-box brace/mount reinforcement, and a good steering stabilizer — especially with larger tires. Correct caster plus tight, beefier linkage eliminates the wobble rather than masking it.
symptoms: Violent front-end shimmy after hitting a bump (death wobble)
Wandering / darting that requires constant correction
Play or slop at the steering wheel
Clunking from the steering box or linkage
Uneven or feathered front tire wear

before.title: Weak light-duty manual transmissions (SR4 / T-4 / T-5)
before.description: The 4-speed SR4 and T-4 and the 5-speed T-5 fitted to many late CJ-7s are light-duty units widely regarded as among the worst transmissions ever put in a CJ. The shift levers are integrated into the tail housing, internals are marginal behind the 258, and shift forks/synchros wear quickly — owners report hard or grinding shifts (notably into 2nd) and short service life, especially once larger tires or any off-road abuse is involved.
before.solution: The bulletproofing answer restorers reach for is replacing the SR4/T-4/T-5 with a stronger gearbox. The T-176 (aluminum-case 4-speed) is the easy upgrade — it bolts in place of the SR4/T-4 with no adapters and gives smooth, durable shifts. For maximum strength behind a 258 or V8, builders fit a Ford-derived T-18 (or NP435/SM465) — the T-18 is considered the toughest factory transmission ever offered in a Jeep — though those need an adapter and a driveshaft-length change. Either way the worn original is retired rather than repeatedly rebuilt.
symptoms: Hard, notchy or grinding shifts, especially into 2nd gear
Popping out of gear
Whine or noise that worsens over time
Worn shift-fork lugs found on teardown
Repeat failures/short life after rebuild
